title: Technical deep dive - unit cost drivers (batching/caching) - AcmeAssist
summary: AcmeAssist asked for a technical walkthrough of what actually moves $/token in production (batching, KV/prefix cache, output length, streaming) and how Redwood measures and reports blended cost internally. Redwood explained the internal definition of blended $/1M output tokens, major attribution inputs (GPU hour rate cards, amortized overhead, dedicated vs hosted allocation), and the main runtime signals used to diagnose changes (cache hit rate, batching utilization, prefill/decode ratio, quantization profile). Customer shared their workload characteristics (chat + agent tool calls, high variance in prompt length, mix of streaming/non-streaming) and concerns about aligning engineering metrics with finance reporting.
topics: Workload profile: QPS, context length distribution, output length, streaming
Continuous batching vs latency SLO tradeoffs
KV/prefix caching: hit rates, eligibility, and how savings show up in unit cost
How Redwood computes blended $/1M output tokens (and why output tokens are the primary denominator)
Dedicated vs hosted allocation differences; idle capacity treatment
Quantization profiles and tagging/guardrails for cost + quality
Reconciliation expectations vs billing and why numbers don’t always match perfectly day-to-day
next_steps: Redwood to send a one-pager on the blended $/1M output tokens definition (inputs/outputs, inclusions/exclusions, streaming parity caveats).
AcmeAssist to share 7-day histograms for input tokens, output tokens, and concurrency, plus target p95 latency and any hard timeouts.
Redwood (Felix) to run a quick sizing worksheet for hosted vs dedicated and recommend initial batching settings for AcmeAssist’s latency targets.
Schedule a follow-up (45 min) to review caching eligibility and a proposed A/B plan (cache on/off) with expected unit cost delta ranges.
action_items: Marissa Cole - email recap with links + propose pilot timeline (end of week) - 2025-01-31
Nadia Rahman - share notes on output token metering nuances for streaming + tool calls (and what Redwood does) - 2025-02-03
Felix Schneider - draft recommended batching configuration ranges given AcmeAssist SLOs (prefill vs decode sensitivity) - 2025-02-04
Jordan Patel (AcmeAssist) - provide workload stats + endpoints list (streaming vs non-streaming split) - 2025-02-05
transcript:
Meeting: Technical deep dive - unit cost drivers (batching/caching) - AcmeAssist
Recorded: 2025-01-29 16:05 PT
Duration: 58 minutes

Attendees
- Redwood Inference: Marissa Cole, Aditya Rao, Nadia Rahman, Felix Schneider
- AcmeAssist: Jordan Patel, Mina Chen, Sam Ortega, Priya Nair

---

[00:00] Marissa Cole: Cool. Okay, we’re recording. Thanks everyone for making time. Today’s goal is to go deeper than the “it depends” answer on cost. Specifically what moves dollars per token in practice, and how we measure it internally so product and finance don’t fight.

[00:14] Jordan Patel: Yeah, that’s exactly it. Our CTO keeps asking “why did cost go up” and engineering answers with GPU utilization charts and it’s like… those don’t reconcile.

[00:26] Priya Nair: And I’m on the finance side trying to translate “utilization” into something that shows up in our cloud bill. So, thank you.

[00:35] Felix Schneider: Totally. And just to set expectations, we can share our internal metric definition and the levers, but the precise numbers depend on your model choice, region, and your latency SLO. But the drivers are fairly consistent.

[00:49] Marissa: Before we jump in, quick intros. I’m Marissa, I run Console & Rollouts product. Aditya is our Optimize lead, Nadia owns token metering, Felix is one of our solutions engineers.

[01:01] Jordan: Jordan, platform. Mina is ML. Sam is backend. Priya is finance ops.

[01:08] Sam Ortega: Hi.

[01:09] Mina Chen: Hey.

[01:11] Marissa: Great. Jordan, do you want to describe your workload quickly? Like QPS, streaming, context sizes.

[01:18] Jordan: Sure. We’re basically an assistant embedded in helpdesk. So chat completions plus tool calls. We stream about… maybe 60% of the time. Prompts can be small like 500 tokens, but can be 8k-ish if the ticket thread is long. Outputs are usually a few hundred tokens, but sometimes we generate longer summaries.

[01:39] Mina: We also do some RAG, so there’s a chunk of retrieved context appended, and that’s where things spike. And we see like bursty traffic. Business hours, basically.

[01:50] Felix: Got it. And latency target? Like p95.

[01:53] Sam: We try to keep p95 under 2.5 seconds to first token for streaming, and under 6 seconds to complete for non-streaming. But it’s not perfectly enforced.

[02:05] Felix: Helpful.

[02:06] Marissa: Okay. So let’s start with the metric. Internally for what this project is driving—our unit economics dashboard—the headline number we use is “blended $ per 1 million output tokens.”

[02:19] Priya: Why output tokens? That’s one of my questions.

[02:23] Nadia Rahman: Yeah. So, two reasons. One: output tokens correlate more directly with compute in decode for most chat workloads, and two: it’s harder to game. Input tokens can be huge from retrieval and that doesn’t always scale cost linearly, especially with caching and prefix reuse. Output is what customers typically experience as value and what varies by temperature and instruction.

[02:44] Mina: But prefill is expensive too. If we shove 8k context, that’s not free.

[02:49] Nadia: Correct. That’s why we don’t ignore input tokens—we track prefill/decode ratio as a driver. But the denominator being output tokens makes comparisons between workloads more stable, and it aligns with how people think about “how much did we generate.”

[03:07] Felix: Also, in practice when teams optimize, they’re trying to reduce cost per response while keeping quality. Responses are mostly driven by output length, plus the prefill overhead.

[03:17] Priya: Okay, so the formula is… what exactly? Like cost divided by output tokens.

[03:23] Marissa: At a high level yes, but “cost” is defined carefully. We use a rate card for GPU hours by region and provider, apply it to measured GPU-time consumption and/or allocated capacity, then add shared overhead allocation (network, storage, control plane), and we split by tier: hosted, dedicated, private. Dedicated and private have different allocation rules.

[03:44] Jordan: When you say “measured GPU time,” are you measuring per request?

[03:48] Felix: Not perfectly per request at the GPU kernel level—there’s too much noise. We do it as an aggregation: tokens and runtime signals per route/model/region/tier, and infrastructure spend inputs per cluster/pool. Then we allocate pool cost to token volumes. That’s what we mean by blended.

[04:09] Priya: So if utilization is low, blended cost goes up.

[04:12] Felix: Exactly. That’s one of the main “surprises.” If you have idle GPU time—because you’ve provisioned for peak or because concurrency dropped—your cost per token rises even if the model is “efficient.”

[04:25] Jordan: That’s like the “idle capacity” question. We were debating whether to treat idle as separate.

[04:31] Marissa: Yep. We track it explicitly as a component. For executive reporting we keep it in the blended metric so it reconciles with spend, but for engineering diagnosis we often show an adjusted view that isolates “effective” cost at observed load. Otherwise you chase ghosts.

[04:49] Sam: That makes sense.

[04:51] Marissa: So, the technical part: what moves blended $/token day to day. It’s basically five buckets: (1) model + quantization profile, (2) batching efficiency, (3) caching, (4) output length / sampling behavior, and (5) allocation effects like region mix and idle.

[05:12] Aditya Rao: I’d add routing/fallbacks too. If your policy falls back to a bigger model during capacity constraints, cost shifts quickly.

[05:19] Jordan: Right, like model substitution.

[05:22] Felix: Exactly.

[05:23] Marissa: Let’s go one by one. Felix, do you want to talk batching first?

[05:28] Felix: Sure. So Redwood’s runtime does continuous batching. At any moment, we can combine multiple requests’ decode steps into a single GPU forward pass. That typically improves tokens/sec per GPU, which lowers $/token.

[05:44] Mina: But batching adds latency because you wait for batch to fill.

[05:48] Felix: Yes. That’s the tradeoff. The knob is “max batch size” and “batching window” (like how long we wait), plus some internal heuristics that depend on model and sequence lengths.

[06:02] Sam: For us, we can’t add too much queueing.

[06:06] Felix: Right. If your SLO is 2.5 seconds to first token, you can’t sit in queue for 400ms. But often we can get gains with very small windows, like 10–30ms, especially at moderate concurrency.

[06:19] Jordan: What’s the metric you look at for batching? Like utilization percentage?

[06:24] Aditya: We use a “batching efficiency” metric, which is basically how close you are to the theoretical max throughput given the model/hardware. Practically it’s: observed tokens/sec divided by expected tokens/sec at a target batch regime, plus “average active sequences per decode step.”

[06:41] Mina: So if we send 1 request at a time, we’re always batch=1, so it’s bad.

[06:45] Felix: Exactly. But also watch out: long-context requests can blow up memory and reduce batch size anyway.

[06:55] Nadia: And that’s where prefill vs decode comes in. Prefill tends to be less batchable in some cases because sequence lengths differ a lot, and you get padding inefficiency.

[07:07] Jordan: Okay.

[07:08] Marissa: Now caching. There are two common layers: request/prompt-level caching and KV/prefix caching.

[07:16] Mina: KV cache is like the transformer attention states, right?

[07:19] Felix: Yeah. If the first N tokens of your prompt repeat, we can reuse the key/value attention cache for that prefix, so the model doesn’t re-compute prefill for that prefix. This is huge for chat where system prompt and tools spec are stable.

[07:36] Sam: We do have a big system prompt, plus tool schemas.

[07:40] Felix: Perfect candidate. If you have, say, 1,500 tokens of stable prefix and your average prompt is 2,000 tokens, that’s a big prefill savings.

[07:51] Jordan: How does that show up in $/token? Because the denominator is output tokens, but the savings is in prefill.

[07:58] Aditya: Exactly. When prefill gets cheaper, your cost per output token drops because total cost per request drops while output stays constant. In our diagnostics we show the prefill/decode ratio and cache hit rates to explain that drop.

[08:14] Mina: Cache “hit rate” is a tricky metric though. What is a hit?

[08:19] Nadia: We define it as: fraction of requests that had a reusable prefix above a threshold, and “tokens saved” as the more important number—how many input tokens were served from cache rather than computed. Two requests could both be “hits,” but one might save 50 tokens, one saves 1500.

[08:38] Priya: So you can translate that to GPU time saved?

[08:42] Felix: Not perfectly linearly, but close enough to attribute directionally. Especially for long contexts.

[08:48] Jordan: And what about response caching? Like exact prompt-to-output caching.

[08:53] Aditya: That’s another layer. Some customers do it at the application layer for deterministic prompts. It’s more brittle for chat, but for embeddings or rerank, it can be huge.

[09:04] Sam: For us, responses are rarely identical, so KV cache seems more relevant.

[09:09] Felix: Agreed.

[09:10] Marissa: Third bucket: model and quantization. If you go from FP16 to int8 or similar, you might reduce compute cost, but there’s quality and sometimes latency differences.

[09:22] Mina: We’ve tested int8 on our side with vLLM. Quality was okay but we had weird edge cases.

[09:28] Felix: Yeah. That’s why we treat quantization as a “profile” tied to a model version. In telemetry we tag it so you can see cost changes are from quantization vs traffic.

[09:40] Nadia: Also important: guardrails on the tag values. Otherwise you end up with a million unique quant profile strings and your metrics backend dies. (laughs)

[09:49] Jordan: Been there.

[09:51] Marissa: Fourth: output length. This sounds obvious, but it’s the biggest driver in many products. If your prompts change, or you roll out a new system message, output tokens can drift +20%, and your $ per 1M output tokens might look stable but your $ per ticket goes up, or vice versa.

[10:10] Priya: So you look at average output tokens per request.

[10:13] Nadia: Yes, and distribution. Long tail matters.

[10:18] Sam: In our case we changed an instruction to “be thorough,” and outputs got longer. So… yeah.

[10:26] Felix: Exactly. And streaming can hide this because people focus on “time to first token,” but you can still produce 2x tokens.

[10:35] Jordan: That’s a good point.

[10:37] Marissa: Fifth bucket: allocation. Region mix, customer tier, dedicated vs hosted. If you route more traffic to a region with higher GPU hour rates, blended unit cost rises.

[10:50] Priya: Like EU is just more expensive.

[10:52] Felix: Often, yes.

[10:54] Jordan: Okay, so let’s talk about measurement. Because our fear is: metrics look great, finance says spend is up.

[11:03] Marissa: Yep. Nadia, can you talk about token metering and what gets counted.

[11:08] Nadia: Sure. At a request level, we meter input tokens and output tokens, plus flags like streaming vs non-streaming, model id, model version, region, tier, route. We aggregate hourly.

[11:23] Mina: Do you count tool calls? Like function calling tokens.

[11:27] Nadia: The tokens are just tokens the model generated in the response, including tool call JSON if it’s in the response stream. Where it gets tricky is streaming: you’re receiving chunks. If instrumentation is only at end-of-stream, you can undercount if clients disconnect or if there’s an error.

[11:46] Sam: That’s literally one of our pain points. Client cancels.

[11:49] Nadia: Yep. We have specific handling to count tokens emitted up to cancellation, but it depends on the gateway path. We’ve been hardening parity across streaming paths. I don’t want to overpromise, but that’s a known area industry-wide.

[12:07] Priya: If tokens are undercounted, your $/1M looks worse, right? Because same cost divided by fewer tokens.

[12:12] Nadia: Exactly. Under-counting output tokens makes unit cost look artificially high.

[12:18] Jordan: That’s the kind of thing we need to detect.

[12:22] Marissa: Internally we run completeness checks. Like, output tokens shouldn’t drop 30% overnight unless traffic dropped, and streaming share changes are tracked.

[12:33] Felix: Also we reconcile dashboard totals against billing totals. Not perfect day-to-day, but close over a week.

[12:41] Priya: Can you explain the reconciliation piece? Because this is my world.

[12:46] Marissa: Sure. Billing is driven by what we invoice: usage by product, commits, overages. The unit economics dashboard is “cost” side: infrastructure spend plus allocations. They’re different, but we still compare usage volumes and token totals to ensure metering is consistent. For finance we care that the “blended cost” number is stable and ties out to recognized spend inputs for the month.

[13:10] Priya: So the dashboard is not our bill, it’s your internal cost.

[13:13] Marissa: Exactly.

[13:15] Jordan: I want to go back to batching. If we do streaming, does batching still help?

[13:20] Felix: Yes, but less predictably. Streaming tends to create more “synchronized” decode steps if requests are similar length. But if you have lots of short responses and long responses mixed, the batch becomes ragged. Continuous batching helps, but you still want concurrency.

[13:39] Sam: We can increase concurrency by queueing, but then time to first token suffers.

[13:44] Felix: So sometimes the best approach is: keep a strict small batching window for the first token path, and allow more aggressive batching after first token—depending on your UX. Some systems do two-tier scheduling.

[13:59] Mina: You can do that?

[14:01] Felix: In some runtimes, yes. Redwood has internal policies around prefill scheduling vs decode scheduling.

[14:08] Jordan: That’s interesting.

[14:10] Aditya: Another lever is request shaping. If you can standardize max output or stop sequences, you reduce variance and batching improves.

[14:20] Sam: We already set max tokens, but it’s generous.

[14:24] Priya: So shorter outputs lowers spend.

[14:26] Sam: Potentially, but it can hurt quality.

[14:28] Marissa: Exactly. That’s why we call it unit economics not just “cost cutting.” You need quality guardrails.

[14:35] Mina: Can we quantify expected savings from KV cache? Like, what’s a realistic range.

[14:41] Felix: It depends on how much of your prompt is stable and how long your prompts are. For chat systems with large system prompt and tools schema, it’s common to save 20–40% of prefill compute. If your prompts are already short, savings are smaller.

[14:58] Jordan: We have a huge tool schema. Like multiple tools.

[15:02] Felix: Then it’s likely meaningful. But you need consistent prefix: same ordering, same whitespace normalization, same tool schema version.

[15:10] Sam: Our tool schema changes occasionally.

[15:13] Nadia: And that’s a telemetry dimension too. If you roll out a new tool schema, cache hit rate can tank and cost jumps. We see that pattern.

[15:24] Mina: So you recommend pinning or versioning that prefix.

[15:27] Felix: Exactly.

[15:29] Jordan: Okay, question: we’ve heard that KV cache can increase memory, reducing batch size. So you win on prefill but lose on batching.

[15:40] Felix: Great question. Yes, caching uses memory. The tradeoff is real. But usually the prefill savings outweighs the batch loss if your prompts are long. For short prompts, it can be net neutral.

[15:55] Aditya: That’s why you want the dashboard signals together: cache hit rate, batching efficiency, and prefill/decode ratio. If cache on -> batching efficiency down but prefill/decode down even more, net win.

[16:10] Priya: That’s the kind of “explainability” we need.

[16:14] Marissa: Right.

[16:16] Mina: How do you compute prefill/decode ratio?

[16:20] Nadia: We approximate by tokens: input tokens (prefill work) vs output tokens (decode work), weighted by model/hardware profile because prefill per token isn’t identical to decode per token. But for diagnostics, raw ratios still correlate with cost.

[16:40] Sam: Is it accurate enough to show “prefill is 60% of cost”?

[16:45] Felix: I would avoid claiming exact percentages unless you have per-kernel profiling. But it’s accurate enough to say “this workload is prefill-heavy, so caching and context reduction are the levers.”

[16:58] Jordan: Makes sense.

[17:00] Marissa: Let’s touch on the internal cost model, since Priya asked. For hosted: we take total GPU spend for the pool (hourly cost * hours), plus overhead, allocate by token volume adjusted by performance profiles. For dedicated: it’s mostly capacity-based, so idle is a big factor.

[17:18] Priya: So if we buy dedicated and don’t use it, our unit cost looks bad.

[17:22] Felix: Right, but that’s “your” unit economics. Dedicated is about predictability and isolation.

[17:28] Jordan: We’re not sure if we need dedicated.

[17:31] Felix: We can help you size it. If you’re bursty, hosted might be better. Dedicated works when you have steadier load or strict data isolation requirements.

[17:42] Mina: Our customers are asking about data retention. Also, some EU customers.

[17:47] Marissa: That’s where region and private/VPC options come in. But cost wise, EU regions can be higher.

[17:55] Priya: That’s… noted. (laughs)

[18:00] Jordan: Okay, can we go through a concrete example? Like, how would you explain a 15% unit cost increase week over week.

[18:08] Aditya: Sure. Typical root causes:
1) Output tokens per request increased (prompt change).
2) Cache hit rate dropped (tool schema change, system prompt change).
3) Traffic shifted to a more expensive region.
4) Batching efficiency dropped (traffic got spikier, more variance, new latency cap).
5) Model version changed or fallback increased.

[18:33] Nadia: And sometimes the boring one: metering gap or missing dimensions causing undercount. If streaming path stops reporting output tokens, unit cost spikes artificially.

[18:44] Sam: That’s scary.

[18:46] Marissa: Yeah, but we put checks around it.

[18:50] Jordan: For our own internal dashboard we have none of that.

[18:54] Felix: This is why we’re building the unit economics dashboard internally—so we can expose this reliably and eventually share a version with customers. But v1 is internal.

[19:08] Priya: Understood.

[19:10] Mina: You mentioned quantization profiles. If we want to test quantization, how do we keep it measurable?

[19:17] Aditya: We’d treat it as: model_id + model_version + quant_profile as separate dimension. Then run A/B: 10% traffic. Track cost per output token, latency, and quality metrics from an eval set.

[19:33] Mina: And if quality dips, we roll back.

[19:36] Aditya: Exactly. And your cache behavior can change too, so watch those metrics.

[19:43] Jordan: Question about tool calls. We have “agent loops” where it calls tools and then continues. Are those separate requests?

[19:50] Sam: Yeah, we do multiple turns.

[19:52] Felix: Right. Then cost per end-user task is sum of multiple completions. If your agent starts doing extra loops, your total spend per ticket goes up, even if $/token stays flat.

[20:07] Priya: That’s actually a key thing. Execs ask cost per ticket.

[20:11] Marissa: Yep. The unit cost dashboard is per token, but you can build product metrics on top.

[20:18] Jordan: I want to make sure I understand: batching helps when concurrency is high; caching helps when prompt prefixes repeat; quantization helps but might impact quality; output length changes everything.

[20:32] Felix: That’s a good summary.

[20:34] Mina: Can we talk more about caching eligibility? Because we have dynamic user context inserted.

[20:40] Felix: Sure. If your prompt is: [system + tools + static instructions] + [dynamic user context] + [question], you can cache the static part. The dynamic part is appended. The more you can push into the static prefix, the better.

[20:58] Sam: We currently inject user profile early.

[21:02] Felix: If you can move it later, or encode it in a smaller way, you’ll increase cached prefix fraction.

[21:09] Mina: But the model might need it earlier for behavior.

[21:13] Felix: True. You have to test. Sometimes you can restructure like: “You will be provided user profile later, follow these rules.” Then append profile.

[21:24] Jordan: Okay.

[21:26] Priya: How do you present this in the dashboard? Like, do you show “cache hit rate” next to cost.

[21:32] Marissa: Yes. The internal dashboard has: blended $/1M output tokens time series, plus top drivers panels. Cache hit rate, batching utilization, average output length, streaming share, quant profile. And then drilldowns by model, region, customer tier.

[21:52] Priya: Nice.

[21:54] Jordan: Are those per route? Like per endpoint.

[21:57] Marissa: We have route dimension but we’re careful about cardinality. For internal we can do route grouping, not raw customer IDs.

[22:06] Sam: That’s good.

[22:08] Mina: We also have a lot of different prompts per product feature, so we’d want that kind of breakdown eventually.

[22:15] Aditya: Yeah. Often you’ll find one “prompt family” generating super long outputs.

[22:22] Jordan: Switching gears slightly: we’ve been told “streaming is more expensive.” Is it?

[22:28] Felix: Streaming isn’t inherently more expensive in compute. It can be more expensive operationally because connections stay open, and it changes batching behavior. But the GPU compute per token is similar.

[22:41] Nadia: The bigger issue is measurement. Streaming has more edge cases: cancellations, partial completions, etc.

[22:50] Sam: We see a lot of client disconnects on mobile.

[22:54] Nadia: Yep, then you must count tokens emitted before disconnect or you’ll undercount output.

[23:00] Priya: Which then breaks the unit metric.

[23:03] Nadia: Correct.

[23:05] Jordan: Okay.

[23:07] Felix: Also, from a latency perspective, streaming can let you accept a bit more batching because users perceive it as faster once the first token arrives. So sometimes you can improve batching without harming UX.

[23:22] Sam: Interesting.

[23:23] Marissa: I’m going to pause and ask: what are you trying to optimize for? Lowest possible cost, or predictable cost, or meeting latency?

[23:33] Jordan: For now, predictable cost. We got surprised by spend last quarter.

[23:38] Priya: Yeah, we can’t have 30% swings.

[23:41] Mina: And we don’t want quality regressions.

[23:44] Felix: Then the approach is: establish baselines, then implement levers one at a time. Caching tends to be low-risk. Batching tuning can be trickier because of latency. Quantization needs evaluation.

[24:00] Jordan: Makes sense.

[24:02] Mina: For caching, do we need to do anything on our side?

[24:06] Felix: Mostly stable prompts and consistent formatting. Redwood handles KV cache internally, but you need to avoid randomizing the prefix. Like, don’t reorder JSON keys in tool schema between requests.

[24:21] Sam: We currently generate tool schema dynamically.

[24:24] Felix: That’s the first thing to fix. Precompute and version it.

[24:29] Jordan: Noted.

[24:31] Priya: Can you also talk about regional cost? Because we’re considering EU deployment.

[24:38] Felix: Sure. Region impacts two things: GPU rate card and sometimes hardware availability. EU-west might have higher $/GPU-hour, and if you’re on newer hardware in one region and older in another, performance per dollar changes. Blended $/token captures that if you drill down by region.

[24:57] Jordan: So you could see “EU is 1.3x US” type thing.

[25:01] Felix: Exactly.

[25:03] Mina: Do you normalize “regions” across providers? Like Azure vs AWS names.

[25:08] Marissa: Internally we do region normalization because otherwise metrics are a mess. We map cloud region labels and internal colo labels to canonical regions.

[25:18] Jordan: Great.

[25:20] Sam: For unit cost, do you include network egress.

[25:25] Marissa: For blended cost, yes, as overhead. Not per request exact, but allocated.

[25:30] Priya: That’s important for finance.

[25:33] Felix: For engineering diagnostics we sometimes separate it so you can see compute vs overhead.

[25:40] Jordan: Okay.

[25:42] Mina: If we do RAG and context is huge, is there any best practice to reduce prefill.

[25:49] Aditya: Yes. Retrieval trimming, reranking, and summarization. But from a unit economics perspective, you can measure it: if input tokens increase but outputs stable, prefill/decode ratio increases and cost per output token rises.

[26:06] Mina: So it’s visible.

[26:08] Aditya: Exactly.

[26:10] Sam: And caching can help if the retrieved chunks repeat.

[26:13] Felix: Potentially, but retrieved docs often differ. More reliable is caching the system prompt and tool schema.

[26:22] Jordan: This is good.

[26:24] Marissa: I want to make sure we hit the original ask: “how Redwood measures $/token internally.” We covered the definition. The key thing is it’s finance-aligned and reconciles with spend, not just GPU profiling.

[26:37] Priya: That’s the key.

[26:39] Marissa: Nadia, anything else on metering details that usually surprises people?

[26:44] Nadia: Two things. One: model identifiers. If model naming changes between runtime and analytics, you end up splitting metrics. We enforce normalized model IDs + versions.

[26:56] Mina: Like “llama-3-70b” vs “Llama3 70B Turbo” nonsense.

[26:59] Nadia: Exactly. Two: high-cardinality dimensions. People want to tag per customer or per prompt, but that will blow up your telemetry. We use controlled dimensions: tier, model, region, route group.

[27:14] Jordan: That’s good to know.

[27:17] Felix: For your use case, you can tag prompt families at the application level and join offline if needed.

[27:24] Sam: Yeah.

[27:26] Priya: Can we shift to “what do we do next” practically? Like, what information do you need from us to estimate savings.

[27:34] Felix: Great. We need: distribution of input tokens, output tokens, concurrency over time (or QPS + p95), percent streaming, and if you have it, cancellation rate. Also which model(s) you’re considering.

[27:52] Jordan: We’re testing a couple open models and also GPT-type models.

[27:57] Felix: Okay. Redwood supports a curated catalog of open models and we can run benchmarks. For this call, we can keep it model-agnostic.

[28:06] Mina: We also have a big system prompt, like 800 tokens, plus tool schema maybe 1200.

[28:12] Felix: That’s a strong caching candidate.

[28:15] Jordan: So next step is you send us the one-pager and we share stats.

[28:20] Marissa: Yep.

[28:21] (crosstalk)

[28:22] Priya: Can the one-pager include what’s included in “overhead” so I can explain it.

[28:28] Marissa: Yes. We’ll include a breakdown: compute (GPU), storage, network, control plane, and how they’re allocated.

[28:36] Priya: Perfect.

[28:38] Mina: Also if you can share what “cache hit rate” definition is.
